nameStory: The clammy locust gets its sticky name from the glandular hairs covering its twigs and leaf stems, which feel distinctly tacky to the touch. When you brush against this tree, you'll understand immediately why early botanists chose 'clammy' to describe it - your fingers will come away feeling like they've touched something slightly adhesive.
description: Clammy locust is a medium-sized deciduous tree that typically grows 20-40 feet tall with an irregular, open crown. Originally from the southeastern United States, this member of the legume family has made its way north and can occasionally be found in New England. Like its relatives, it produces showy clusters of pink to rose-colored flowers that look like sweet pea blossoms, followed by brown seed pods that split open to release their seeds.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, drooping clusters of pink to rose-colored pea-like flowers appear in late spring to early summer, each bloom about an inch long with the characteristic irregular shape of legume flowers

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-21 oval leaflets arranged along a central stem, each leaflet 1-2 inches long with smooth edges and a slightly fuzzy underside

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young twigs and branches feel distinctly sticky or tacky due to glandular hairs - this clammy texture is the tree's signature feature and where it gets its name

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Brown, flattened seed pods 2-4 inches long that are also covered in sticky glandular hairs and split open along two seams when mature

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Medium-sized tree with an open, irregular crown and branches that tend to be somewhat brittle, often forming thickets through root sprouting

habitat: In New England, clammy locust is most often found in disturbed areas, along roadsides, and in open woodlands, particularly on well-drained soils. As a non-native species that's occasionally planted for ornamental purposes, it may escape cultivation and establish in sunny locations. It tolerates poor soils and can colonize areas where other trees struggle.

seasonality.spring: Compound leaves emerge in late spring, followed by showy pink flower clusters that bloom from May into June, attracting bees and other pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Flowers give way to developing seed pods while the full canopy of compound leaves provides filtered shade. The sticky texture of twigs is most noticeable during active growing season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow before dropping, and mature seed pods begin to split open and release their seeds.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the tree's open growth habit, with persistent seed pods often remaining attached and the sticky residue on twigs still detectable on warmer days.

funFact: The sticky glands covering clammy locust's twigs and pods may actually serve as a natural pest control system - small insects can get trapped in the tacky secretions, potentially protecting the tree from some herbivorous bugs!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with black locust, but clammy locust's pink flowers (versus white in black locust) and distinctly sticky twigs make identification straightforward - just touch a young branch and you'll know immediately which species you've found.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'locust,' this tree is actually a member of the legume family and completely unrelated to the grasshopper-like insects of the same name. The name comes from the tree's hard wood, which early settlers thought resembled the carob pods (also called locust beans) mentioned in biblical stories.
compareHints: Among the locust trees, clammy locust stands out with its pink flowers and sticky twigs, while black locust has white flowers and smooth branches. Bristly locust is much smaller (usually shrub-sized) and has bristly rather than sticky hairs, plus it rarely reaches tree proportions in New England.
